Surah 90: Al-Balad (The City)
It is Meccan, and it has twenty verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

(p-473) ﴿I swear by this city﴾ ﴿while you are a resident of this city﴾ [Al-Balad: 2] ﴿and by the begetter and what he begot﴾ [Al-Balad: 3] ﴿Indeed, We created man in toil﴾ [Al-Balad: 4] ﴿Does he think that no one will have power over him?﴾ [Al-Balad: 5] ﴿He says, "I have squandered wealth in abundance."﴾ [Al-Balad: 6] ﴿Does he think that no one sees him?﴾ [Al-Balad: 7] ﴿Have We not made for him two eyes﴾ [Al-Balad: 8] ﴿and a tongue and two lips?﴾ [Al-Balad: 9] ﴿And have We not shown him the two highways?﴾ [Al-Balad: 10] ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾ [Al-Balad: 11] ﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is?﴾ [Al-Balad: 12] ﴿It is freeing a neck [from bondage]﴾ [Al-Balad: 13] ﴿or feeding on a day of severe hunger﴾ [Al-Balad: 14] ﴿an orphan of near relationship﴾ [Al-Balad: 15] ﴿or a needy person in misery﴾ [Al-Balad: 16] ﴿Then he is among those who believed and advised one another to patience and advised one another to compassion﴾ [Al-Balad: 17] ﴿Those are the companions of the right hand﴾ [Al-Balad: 18] ﴿And those who disbelieved in Our signs, they are the companions of the left hand﴾ [Al-Balad: 19] ﴿Over them will be a fire sealed shut﴾ [Al-Balad: 20].

Al-kabad (kabad): hardship and difficulty. Its origin is from the phrase kabida al-rajul kabadan, fa-huwa akbad, when his liver (kabid) afflicted him and swelled up. It was then used for every toil and hardship, and from it comes al-mukabada (struggle). Labid said:

Ya ʿaynu hallā bakayti Arbada idh qumnā wa qāma al-khuṣūmu fī kabad

And Abu al-Asba' said:

Wa-li ibnu ʿammin law anna al-nāsa fī kabad ∗∗∗ labaẓẓa muḥtajizan bil-nabli yarmīnī

Al-shafah (lip) is well known, and its original form is shafahah, from which the letter ha' was deleted. This is indicated by shufayhah, shifāh, and shāfahtu. It is among the words whose plural cannot be formed with the alif and ta' suffix, even though it has the ta' of feminine marking.

Al-najd: the neck, its plural is nujūd, and by it Najd was named because of its elevation above the lowland of Tihamah. Al-najd also means the high road. Imru' al-Qays said:

Farīqāni minhum jāzi‘un baṭna Nakhlata wa ākharu minhum qāṭi‘un najda Kabkabi

Al-fakk: freeing a thing from another thing. The poet said:

Fa-yā rubba makrūbin karartu warāʾahu ∗∗∗ wa ʿānin fakaktu al-ghulla ʿanhu fa-qaddānī

Al-saghab: general hunger, and it may be said sagiba al-rajul when he became hungry. Taraba al-rajul means when a man became poor and clung to the dust, and atraba means when he became wealthy and had property like dust; similarly athrā. Awṣadtu al-bāb and āṣadtuhu mean when you closed and sealed the door. The poet said:

Taḥinnu ilā ajbāli Makkata nāqatī ∗∗∗ wa min dūnihā abwābu Ṣanʿāʾa mu'ṣadah

(p-474) This surah is Meccan according to the majority, and it has been said that it is Medinan. When Almighty Allah mentioned His testing of man through a state of ease and a state of restriction, and mentioned some of his blameworthy characteristics and what his condition and the condition of the believer led to, He followed it with a type of his testing, his bad condition, and what he will come to in the Hereafter. The reference to "this city" is to Makkah.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 90, verses 2–3:

﴿And you are a resident (ḥillun) in this city﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya) which conveys the magnification of that by which He swears, meaning: "so you are residing in it." This is the apparent meaning. Ibn ʿAbbas and a group said its meaning is: "And you are lawful (ḥalāl) in this city, it being lawful for you to kill whomever you wish within it," and this was on the day of the conquest of Makkah. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is built upon the view of those who say that lā is negating, meaning that this city is not one by which God swears, and its people have committed deeds that necessitate the making lawful (ihlāl) of its sanctity." Shuraḥbīl ibn Saʿd said: "It means ﴿And you are a resident in this city﴾, they have made you lawful, the one whose harm, killing and expulsion are made permissible." This view was begun by al-Zamakhshari, who said: "In it is an incitement to bear what he endured from the people of Makkah, and an expression of wonder at their state in their enmity towards him; or it consoles the Messenger of God ﷺ, by swearing by his city, that a human being is never free of enduring hardships." He objected that God promised him the conquest of Makkah as a completion of the consolation and relief for him, so [the verse means]: "And you will be a resident in it in the future, doing in it whatever you want of killing and taking captives."

Then al-Zamakhshari said, after a lengthy discussion: "If you ask: where is the parallel to His saying ﴿And you are a resident﴾ in the sense of the future? I say: His saying, mighty and majestic, ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30], is widespread in the speech of people; you say to one whom you promise honour and gifts: 'And you are honoured and beloved,' and it is wider in the speech of God, because future states are with Him like the present and witnessed. And let it suffice you as conclusive proof that it is for the future, and that interpreting it as the present is impossible: the surah is by agreement Meccan, and where is the emigration (hijra) from the time of its revelation? So what of the conquest?" End of quote.

Taking it as a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍiyya) is not determined; we mentioned at the outset that it is a circumstantial clause, and we explained the goodness of its placement. It is a contemporaneous circumstance (ḥāl muqārana), not an anticipated one (muqaddara) nor a narrated one (maḥkiyya), so it is not one of the reports of the future. As for his question and answer, one who has even slight connection with grammar would not ask this, because reports may concern future events, and the active participle (ism al-fā'il) and what goes in its wake, when it is predicated or used as a description, is not determined to be taken as present; rather it may refer to the past at times, to the present at others, and to the future at others. This is from the basics of the science of grammar. As for his saying "And let it suffice you as conclusive proof…", it is nothing, because we did not take ﴿And you are a resident﴾ to mean that what you do in Makkah of captivity and killing is lawful for you at the time of its revelation in Makkah, so that they would contradict; rather we took it to mean that he is residing in it specifically, and at the time of revelation he was residing in it by necessity. Also, what he reports of the consensus that it was revealed in Makkah is not correct, and the disagreement concerning it has been related from the statement of Ibn ʿAṭiyya. The saying ﴿And you are a resident in this city﴾ does not indicate what they mentioned, that the meaning is that he is making things lawful at that time, nor that you make lawful things in it. Rather the apparent meaning is what we mentioned at the outset: that He, exalted is He, swore by it for the two nobilities it combines: its nobility through its attribution to God, exalted is He, and its nobility through the presence of the Messenger of God ﷺ and his residence in it, so it became fit to be sworn by.

Apparently His saying ﴿And a begetter and what he begot﴾ does not refer to a specific individual, but applies to every begetter. Ibn ʿAbbas said this, saying: "It is general, encompassing all living beings." Mujahid said: "Adam and all his offspring." It was also said: "and the righteous among his descendants." It was said: "Noah and his descendants." Abu ʿImran al-Hawfi said: "Abraham, peace be upon him, and all his offspring." It was said: "the begetter of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and what he begot is Abraham, peace be upon him." Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi said: "It is possible that the begetter is the Prophet ﷺ, due to the prior mention of him, and what he begot is his ummah, based on his saying ﷺ: '(Indeed I am to you in the position of a father)', and on the reading of ʿAbd Allah: (And his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them)." So He swore by him and by his ummah after He swore by his city, magnifying his nobility, upon him be prayers and peace. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is meant by a begetter and what he begot? I say: the Messenger of God ﷺ and whoever he begot. He swore by his city, which is the place of his birth, the sanctuary of his father Abraham, and the place where his father Ishmael grew up, peace be upon them both, and by whom he begot and by him. If you ask: why was it indefinite? I say: for the independent indefiniteness that carries praise and wonder. If you ask: why not say 'and who he begot'? I say: it has the same as in His saying ﴿And God knows best what she delivered﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 36], meaning: 'with what she delivered,' that is, a thing of wondrous state." End of quote.

al-Farra' said: "What (mā) has the sense of who (man) as in His saying ﴿what seems good to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 3] and ﴿and He who created the male and female﴾ [al-Layl: 3], and He is the Creator of the male and female." End of quote.

Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima and Ibn Jubayr said: the intended "begetter" is one who can beget, and "what he begot" is the barren one who cannot beget. They took mā as negating, so it requires supplying a relative pronoun that makes this meaning valid, as if he said: "a begetter and the one who did not beget." The omission of the relative pronoun is not permitted according to the Basrans.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 90, verses 4–20:

﴿We have certainly created man in toil.﴾ This is the sentence about which the oath is sworn. The majority hold that "al-insan" (man) is a generic noun (ism jins). "In kabad" means that he struggles with the hardships of this world and the Hereafter. His hardships cannot be counted, from the cutting of his umbilical cord until he settles in his final abode: either in Paradise, where hardships depart from him, or in the Fire, where his hardships and severities are multiplied. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah ibn Shaddad, Abu Salih, al-Dahhak and Mujahid said: "﴿in kabad﴾" means standing upright, and that he was not created prone on his face. This is a favour bestowed upon him. Ibn Kaysan said: his head is upright in his mother's belly, and when he is permitted to come out, he turns his head toward his mother's feet. From Ibn 'Umar: he struggles to give thanks in times of ease, and he struggles to be patient in times of hardship. Ibn Zayd said: "al-insan" is Adam, and "﴿in kabad﴾" means in the sky, which he called kabad. These opinions are weak. The first is the apparent meaning.

The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "(a-yahsabu)" [does he think] refers to "al-insan." That is, because of his stubbornness, his might and his strength, he thinks that no one can withstand him, and that no one can overpower him, relying on his numbers and his equipment. He says in boastful manner: ﴿I have squandered wealth in abundance.﴾ That is, in noble deeds and whatever brings praise. Does he think that his deeds are hidden, and that no one sees him or is aware of him in his spending and in the purpose of what he seeks, of which nothing is for the sake of Allah? Rather, over him are guardians who record what proceeds from him of deeds during his life, and they keep count of them until the Day of Recompense.

It was also said that the pronoun in "(a-yahsabu)" refers to some of the chiefs of Quraysh. It was said that it refers to Abu al-Asad Usayd ibn Kalada, who would have a Ukaziyy leather mat spread out for him, and he would stand upon it and say: "Whoever moves me from it, for him is such-and-such." So it would not be removed except in pieces, and the place of his two feet would remain. It was also said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It was also said: al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal, who, whenever he sinned, would seek a fatwa from the Prophet (ﷺ), and he would order him to make expiation. So he said: "I have squandered wealth in abundance in expiations and obligations since I followed Muhammad (ﷺ)."

The majority recited "lubadan" with a damma on the lam and a fatha on the ba'. Abu Ja'far recited it with a shadda on the ba' (lubbadan). From him and from Zayd ibn 'Ali: "lubdan" with a sukun on the ba'. Mujahid and Ibn Abi al-Zinad recited it with a damma on both letters (lubudan).

Then He enumerated upon man His blessings, saying: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes?﴾ with which he sees; ﴿and a tongue﴾ which expresses what is within his inner self; ﴿and two lips?﴾ which he closes over his mouth, and with which he is helped in eating, drinking, blowing, and other things.

﴿And We guided him to the two highways.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: the path of good and the path of evil. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did 'Ali, Ibn al-Musayyab and al-Dahhak: the two breasts, because they are like the two paths for the life and sustenance of the child.

﴿But he has not attempted the ascent.﴾ That is, he has not given thanks for those past blessings. "Al-'aqaba" (the steep ascent) is a metaphor (isti'ara) for this deed, which is arduous upon the self in that it is the expenditure of wealth; it is a comparison (tashbih) with the steep path of a mountain, which is the difficult part of it, and it is an ascent, for one encounters hardship in traversing it. "Iqtahamaha" means he entered it swiftly, with pressure and intensity. "Al-quhma" means severity, and a severe year. It is said: "qahama fi al-amr qu-humaan" means he threw himself into the matter without deliberation. The apparent meaning is that "la" is for negation, and this is the view of Abu 'Ubayda, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, as if He said: "We gave him the limbs and guided him to the way, yet he did not do good," that is, he did not attempt. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "la" is mentioned only once, and the Arabs rarely use "la" alone with the past tense without repeating it, as in His saying: ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed﴾ [al-Qiyama: 31]. He only mentioned it once because the end of the sentence indicates its meaning. So it is possible that His saying ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ stands in the place of the repetition, as if He said: "He did not attempt the ascent, nor did he believe." It was also said: it is in the manner of supplication, like the saying "la naja wa la salima" (may he not be saved, nor safe), a prayer against him that he not do good. It was also said: it is an exhortation (tahdid) with "la," and we do not know of "la" alone being used for exhortation without the hamza accompanying it. It was also said: "al-'aqaba" is Hell, from which none is saved except by these deeds; this was said by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ka'b said: it is a mountain in Hell. Al-Zamakhshari, after adopting the view of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, said: "la" here carries the meaning of a repeated "la," because the meaning of ﴿He did not attempt the ascent﴾ is: "He did not free a neck, nor feed a poor man in a day of hunger." Do you not see that he explained the ascent by this? End of quotation. This is not complete for him except according to the reading of the one who reads "faka" as a past verb.

Ibn Kathir and the two grammarians (al-Nahwiyyan) read "faka" as a past verb, with "raqabatan" in the accusative; or "aṭ'ama" as a past verb. The rest of the seven read "fakku" in the nominative, "raqabatin" in the genitive, and "it'am" as a verbal noun (masdar) with tanwin, conjoined to "fakku." 'Ali and Abu Raja' recited like the reading of Ibn Kathir, except that they read "dha masghabatin" with an alif. Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' also recited "(aw it'amun fi yawmin dha)" with an alif, and the accusative of "dha" as the object, meaning a person who is in hunger. "Yatiman" is a substitute (badal) for it or a qualifier (sifa). Some of the Successors (tabi'un) recited "fakku raqabatin" with the genitive construction, and "aw aṭ'ama" as a past verb. As for the one who reads "fakku" in the nominative, it is an explanation of "iqtiham al-'aqaba," and the implied sense is: "And what will make you know what the ascent is?" As for the one who reads a past verb, there is no need to posit an omitted noun; rather the glorification is of the ascent itself, and "faka" comes as a substitute for "iqtaham." This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya. The freeing of a neck is its liberation from captivity and bondage.

﴿An orphan of near relationship,﴾ so that charity and kinship are combined. Here "aw" is for variety (tanwi'). The description of a day as "one of hunger" is by way of extension (ittisa').

﴿Or a needy person in misery.﴾ He said: they are those cast onto the side of the road, sitting upon the dust, having no homes. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the one who leaves his house, then turns his face toward it, certain that there is nothing in it but dust.

﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾: this is conjoined to His saying ﴿so he did not attempt﴾. "Thumma" (then) enters for the delay of faith and virtue, not for a delay in time, because faith must precede those good deeds, since it is a condition for their validity when performed by one who obeys. Or the meaning is: then, in the end of his affair, he was among those who met death in faith, since being met by death upon faith is a condition for benefiting from acts of obedience. Or the delay is in the mention, as if it were said: "Then mention that he was among those who believed."

﴿And advised one another to patience,﴾ that is, some of them enjoined upon others patience in faith, in acts of obedience, and in abstaining from sins.

﴿And advised one another to compassion,﴾ that is, to mutual kindness and mercy, or to that which leads to the mercy of Allah.

"Al-maymana" (the right) and "al-mash'ama" (the left) have already been discussed in al-Waqi'a.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza and Hafs recited "mu'sada" (closed) with a hamza here and in al-Humaza. It appears that it is from "aṣadtu" (I closed). It was said: it is possible that it is from "awṣadtu," and the hamza was inserted in accordance with those who recite "al-su'q" with a hamza. The rest of the seven recited without a hamza, and it appears that it is from "awṣadtu." It was said: it is possible that it is from "aṣadtu," and the hamza was softened. A poet said:

*Folk whose sons treat their lice,*
*and chains of rings, and a door closed fast.*

﴿And We guided him to the two highways.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: the path of good and the path of evil. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did 'Ali, Ibn al-Musayyab and al-Dahhak: the two breasts, because they are like the two paths for the life and sustenance of the child.

﴿But he has not attempted the ascent.﴾ That is, he has not given thanks for those past blessings. "Al-'aqaba" (the steep ascent) is a metaphor (isti'ara) for this deed, which is arduous upon the self in that it is the expenditure of wealth; it is a comparison (tashbih) with the steep path of a mountain, which is the difficult part of it, and it is an ascent, for one encounters hardship in traversing it. "Iqtahamaha" means he entered it swiftly, with pressure and intensity. "Al-quhma" means severity, and a severe year. It is said: "qahama fi al-amr qu-humaan" means he threw himself into the matter without deliberation. The apparent meaning is that "la" is for negation, and this is the view of Abu 'Ubayda, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, as if He said: "We gave him the limbs and guided him to the way, yet he did not do good," that is, he did not attempt. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "la" is mentioned only once, and the Arabs rarely use "la" alone with the past tense without repeating it, as in His saying: ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed﴾ [al-Qiyama: 31]. He only mentioned it once because the end of the sentence indicates its meaning. So it is possible that His saying ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ stands in the place of the repetition, as if He said: "He did not attempt the ascent, nor did he believe." It was also said: it is in the manner of supplication, like the saying "la naja wa la salima" (may he not be saved, nor safe), a prayer against him that he not do good. It was also said: it is an exhortation (tahdid) with "la," and we do not know of "la" alone being used for exhortation without the hamza accompanying it. It was also said: "al-'aqaba" is Hell, from which none is saved except by these deeds; this was said by al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ka'b said: it is a mountain in Hell. Al-Zamakhshari, after adopting the view of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, said: "la" here carries the meaning of a repeated "la," because the meaning of ﴿He did not attempt the ascent﴾ is: "He did not free a neck, nor feed a poor man in a day of hunger." Do you not see that he explained the ascent by this? End of quotation. This is not complete for him except according to the reading of the one who reads "faka" as a past verb.

Ibn Kathir and the two grammarians (al-Nahwiyyan) read "faka" as a past verb, with "raqabatan" in the accusative; or "aṭ'ama" as a past verb. The rest of the seven read "fakku" in the nominative, "raqabatin" in the genitive, and "it'am" as a verbal noun (masdar) with tanwin, conjoined to "fakku." 'Ali and Abu Raja' recited like the reading of Ibn Kathir, except that they read "dha masghabatin" with an alif. Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' also recited "(aw it'amun fi yawmin dha)" with an alif, and the accusative of "dha" as the object, meaning a person who is in hunger. "Yatiman" is a substitute (badal) for it or a qualifier (sifa). Some of the Successors (tabi'un) recited "fakku raqabatin" with the genitive construction, and "aw aṭ'ama" as a past verb. As for the one who reads "fakku" in the nominative, it is an explanation of "iqtiham al-'aqaba," and the implied sense is: "And what will make you know what the ascent is?" As for the one who reads a past verb, there is no need to posit an omitted noun; rather the glorification is of the ascent itself, and "faka" comes as a substitute for "iqtaham." This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya. The freeing of a neck is its liberation from captivity and bondage.

﴿An orphan of near relationship,﴾ so that charity and kinship are combined. Here "aw" is for variety (tanwi'). The description of a day as "one of hunger" is by way of extension (ittisa').

﴿Or a needy person in misery.﴾ He said: they are those cast onto the side of the road, sitting upon the dust, having no homes. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the one who leaves his house, then turns his face toward it, certain that there is nothing in it but dust.

﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾: this is conjoined to His saying ﴿so he did not attempt﴾. "Thumma" (then) enters for the delay of faith and virtue, not for a delay in time, because faith must precede those good deeds, since it is a condition for their validity when performed by one who obeys. Or the meaning is: then, in the end of his affair, he was among those who met death in faith, since being met by death upon faith is a condition for benefiting from acts of obedience. Or the delay is in the mention, as if it were said: "Then mention that he was among those who believed."

﴿And advised one another to patience,﴾ that is, some of them enjoined upon others patience in faith, in acts of obedience, and in abstaining from sins.

﴿And advised one another to compassion,﴾ that is, to mutual kindness and mercy, or to that which leads to the mercy of Allah.

"Al-maymana" (the right) and "al-mash'ama" (the left) have already been discussed in al-Waqi'a.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza and Hafs recited "mu'sada" (closed) with a hamza here and in al-Humaza. It appears that it is from "aṣadtu" (I closed). It was said: it is possible that it is from "awṣadtu," and the hamza was inserted in accordance with those who recite "al-su'q" with a hamza. The rest of the seven recited without a hamza, and it appears that it is from "awṣadtu." It was said: it is possible that it is from "aṣadtu," and the hamza was softened. A poet said:

*Folk whose sons treat their lice,*
*and chains of rings, and a door closed fast.*
